q: In ballet, what does the term 'plie' mean?
fact: Plie comes from the French verb plier, meaning to bend.

q: How many basic positions of the feet are there in classical ballet?
fact: Classical ballet codifies five basic positions of the feet.

q: What does 'jete' translate to in English?
fact: Jete means thrown, describing a leap where a leg is thrown into the air.

q: Which composer wrote the music for Swan Lake?
fact: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky composed Swan Lake, first staged in 1877.

q: The Sugar Plum Fairy appears in which ballet?
fact: The Sugar Plum Fairy dances a famous celesta solo in The Nutcracker.

q: What does 'pas de deux' mean?
fact: A pas de deux is a dance for two, usually a duet for a lead couple.

q: Which modern dance pioneer built a technique around contraction and release?
fact: Martha Graham's technique centers on the contraction and release of the torso.

q: Which choreographer famously used chance procedures to build dances?
fact: Merce Cunningham used coin tosses and other chance methods to order movement.

q: What is Alvin Ailey's most famous work?
fact: Revelations, premiered in 1960, is Ailey's signature work.

q: What does 'fouette' mean?
fact: Fouette means whipped, describing the whipping action of the working leg.

q: How many fouette turns does Odile traditionally perform in Swan Lake?
fact: The Black Swan coda traditionally features 32 fouette turns.

q: Which choreographer is known for turned-in knees, rolled shoulders and bowler hats?
fact: Bob Fosse's style shaped Chicago, Cabaret and Sweet Charity.

q: What does 'tendu' mean?
fact: Tendu means stretched, with the foot sliding out without lifting off the floor.

q: Ballet vocabulary is standardized in which language?
fact: Ballet terms were codified in French at the court of Louis XIV.

q: Who founded New York City Ballet and is called the father of American ballet?
fact: George Balanchine co-founded New York City Ballet in 1948.

q: Which Balanchine ballet was the first he created in America?
fact: Serenade, made in 1934, was Balanchine's first ballet created in the United States.

q: Who choreographed the dream ballet in the musical Oklahoma!?
fact: Agnes de Mille's 1943 dream ballet changed how dance was used in musicals.

q: Who choreographed the original West Side Story?
fact: Jerome Robbins choreographed and directed the 1957 original production.

q: Who conceived and choreographed A Chorus Line?
fact: Michael Bennett built A Chorus Line from taped sessions with Broadway dancers.

q: What makes the sound in tap shoes?
fact: Metal plates are screwed onto the toe and heel of the shoe.

q: Which tap dancer starred in the 1989 film Tap?
fact: Gregory Hines led the film, with Sammy Davis Jr in a supporting role.

q: Who created and starred in Bring in da Noise, Bring in da Funk?
fact: Savion Glover choreographed the 1996 show and won a Tony Award for it.

q: In which California city did popping originate?
fact: Popping developed in Fresno, largely through Boogaloo Sam and the Electric Boogaloos.

q: Where did breaking originate in the 1970s?
fact: Breaking grew out of block party culture in the Bronx, New York.

q: At which Olympic Games did breaking debut as a medal sport?
fact: Breaking made its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games.

q: Voguing came out of which scene?
fact: Voguing developed in Harlem's Black and Latino ballroom scene.

q: Which documentary chronicled New York ballroom culture?
fact: Paris Is Burning was released in 1990 and documented Harlem drag balls.

q: Who developed the Gaga movement language?
fact: Ohad Naharin developed Gaga while leading Batsheva Dance Company.

q: Pina Bausch led which company?
fact: Pina Bausch directed Tanztheater Wuppertal from 1973 until her death in 2009.

q: Which dancer is called the mother of modern dance and performed barefoot?
fact: Isadora Duncan rejected ballet's corsets and shoes for free, natural movement.

q: What does 'port de bras' refer to?
fact: Port de bras means the carriage or movement of the arms.

q: In an arabesque, where is the working leg?
fact: An arabesque extends one leg straight behind the body.

q: What does 'releve' mean?
fact: Releve means raised, rising onto the balls of the feet or onto pointe.

q: What does 'chasse' mean?
fact: A chasse is a gliding step where one foot chases the other.

q: What is the stiffened toe of a pointe shoe called?
fact: The box is built from layers of fabric, paper and glue hardened into a rigid toe.

q: Proper turnout in ballet rotates from which joint?
fact: Turnout comes from external rotation at the hip, never from twisting the knees.

q: What technique keeps dancers from getting dizzy while turning?
fact: Spotting means snapping the head around to fix the eyes on one point.

q: Who was the impresario behind the Ballets Russes?
fact: Sergei Diaghilev founded and directed the Ballets Russes from 1909.

q: Whose 1913 premiere of The Rite of Spring caused an uproar in Paris?
fact: Nijinsky choreographed the Stravinsky score, and the 1913 premiere caused a famous scandal.

q: In Giselle, what are the Wilis?
fact: The Wilis are the vengeful spirits of women who died before their wedding day.

q: Which Russian dancer defected in 1974 and later directed American Ballet Theatre?
fact: Baryshnikov defected in Toronto in 1974 and led ABT in the 1980s.

q: Which dancer made a famous defection in Paris in 1961?
fact: Rudolf Nureyev defected at Le Bourget airport in June 1961.

q: Who became the first Black female principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre?
fact: Misty Copeland was promoted to principal at ABT in 2015.

q: Who choreographed the Broadway musical Hamilton?
fact: Andy Blankenbuehler won a Tony Award for choreographing Hamilton in 2016.

q: Who starred in and co-directed Singin' in the Rain?
fact: Gene Kelly co-directed the 1952 film with Stanley Donen and danced the title number.

q: Who was Fred Astaire's most famous screen dance partner?
fact: Astaire and Ginger Rogers made ten films together.

q: Riverdance showcases which dance form?
fact: Riverdance grew out of a 1994 Eurovision interval act led by Michael Flatley and Jean Butler.

q: Flamenco comes from which region of Spain?
fact: Flamenco developed in Andalusia in southern Spain.

q: Bharatanatyam is a classical dance form from which country?
fact: Bharatanatyam originated in the temples of Tamil Nadu in southern India.

q: What is the time signature of a waltz?
fact: A waltz is counted in three, written in 3/4 time.

q: What does 'grand jete' describe?
fact: A grand jete is a big leap, often with the legs reaching a split in the air.

q: What does 'pirouette' mean in French?
fact: Pirouette means to whirl or spin, describing a turn on one leg.

q: Which muscles power a releve?
fact: The gastrocnemius and soleus in the calf lift the heels through the Achilles tendon.

q: Where are the hamstrings located?
fact: The hamstrings run down the back of the thigh from the hip to below the knee.

q: Which is the largest muscle in the human body?
fact: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle by volume and extends the hip.

q: What does 'sickling' the foot mean?
fact: Sickling twists the foot out of alignment with the leg and strains the ankle.

q: What does the injury protocol RICE stand for?
fact: RICE is the classic first response to a sprain or strain.

q: Plantar fasciitis causes pain in which part of the body?
fact: It is inflammation of the band of tissue running along the bottom of the foot.

q: Which joint do dancers most commonly injure?
fact: Ankle sprains are the most frequently reported dance injury.

q: Which tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone?
fact: The Achilles is the thickest and strongest tendon in the human body.

q: Which TV competition show premiered on Fox in 2005?
choices: So You Think You Can Dance
fact: So You Think You Can Dance premiered in July 2005.

q: Who hosted the NBC series World of Dance?
fact: Jenna Dewan hosted World of Dance, while Jennifer Lopez was a judge and producer.

q: In competition dance, what does adjudication mean?
fact: Adjudicated awards give each routine a level rather than only a placement.

q: What is a 'go-see' in the commercial dance world?
fact: A go-see is a short casting appointment, often arranged through an agent.

q: What does 'call time' mean on a job?
fact: Call time is the required arrival time, not the start of performance.

q: Which union covers performers in film and television in the US?
fact: SAG-AFTRA was formed in 2012 by the merger of SAG and AFTRA.

q: Which union represents stage actors and stage managers on Broadway?
fact: Actors Equity Association was founded in 1913.

q: What does a dance captain do?
fact: The dance captain keeps the choreography clean and rehearses replacements.

q: What is a 'swing' in a musical?
choices: A performer who covers several ensemble tracks
fact: Swings learn multiple ensemble tracks and go on when someone is out.

q: What is an understudy?
choices: Someone who covers a principal role
fact: An understudy is prepared to step into a named role at short notice.

q: What is a dance reel?
choices: A short edited video of your dancing
fact: Agents and casting directors usually ask for a reel under two minutes.

q: What is the standard printed headshot size in the US?
fact: US headshots are traditionally printed at 8 by 10 inches with the resume on the back.

q: Who choreographed the Single Ladies video for Beyonce?
fact: JaQuel Knight choreographed Single Ladies in 2008 and later copyrighted the choreography.

q: Beyonce's 2018 Coachella performance was released as which film?
fact: Homecoming premiered on Netflix in 2019.

q: Which Janet Jackson album produced the Rhythm Nation video?
fact: Janet Jackson's Rhythm Nation 1814 was released in 1989.

q: Who directed the Thriller music video?
fact: John Landis directed the 14-minute Thriller video, released in 1983.

q: Which pop star began her career choreographing for the Laker Girls?
fact: Paula Abdul was a Laker Girl and then their choreographer before her recording career.

q: Who choreographed Dirty Dancing and later directed High School Musical?
fact: Kenny Ortega choreographed Dirty Dancing in 1987 and directed High School Musical in 2006.

q: Which 2000 film follows students at a fictional New York ballet academy?
fact: Center Stage cast real dancers including Amanda Schull and Ethan Stiefel.

q: Who starred as the lead in the 2010 film Black Swan?
fact: Natalie Portman won the Academy Award for Best Actress for the role.

q: Which actor starred in the first Step Up film in 2006?
fact: Channing Tatum starred opposite Jenna Dewan in the 2006 original.

q: Save the Last Dance starred which actress as an aspiring ballet dancer?
fact: Julia Stiles starred opposite Sean Patrick Thomas in the 2001 film.

q: The reality series Dance Moms was set at a studio in which city?
fact: Abby Lee Miller's studio was in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

q: In which year did The Nutcracker premiere?
fact: The Nutcracker premiered in St Petersburg in December 1892.

q: Which composer wrote The Sleeping Beauty?
fact: Tchaikovsky wrote all three of his great ballets: Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker.

q: Who composed the score for the ballet Coppelia?
fact: Leo Delibes composed Coppelia, premiered in Paris in 1870.

q: Who composed the ballets Don Quixote and La Bayadere?
fact: Ludwig Minkus wrote both scores for Marius Petipa.

q: Who composed the ballet Romeo and Juliet?
fact: Prokofiev's Romeo and Juliet includes the famous Dance of the Knights.

q: Which Copland score did Martha Graham choreograph?
fact: Appalachian Spring premiered in 1944 with Graham dancing the Bride.

q: Agnes de Mille choreographed which Aaron Copland ballet?
fact: Rodeo premiered in 1942 with de Mille dancing the Cowgirl.

q: Twyla Tharp built the Broadway show Movin' Out around which musician's songs?
fact: Movin' Out opened in 2002 and used Billy Joel's catalog.

q: Who choreographed the original Broadway production of Cats?
fact: Gillian Lynne choreographed Cats, which opened in London in 1981.

q: Which choreographer is known for Kinky Boots and Legally Blonde?
fact: Jerry Mitchell won a Tony for La Cage aux Folles and choreographed Kinky Boots.

q: When was Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater founded?
fact: Alvin Ailey founded the company in New York in 1958.

q: Which Ailey dancer performed the solo Cry and later led the company?
fact: Alvin Ailey created Cry for Judith Jamison in 1971; she became artistic director in 1989.

q: Which dancer was also an anthropologist and created a named technique?
fact: Katherine Dunham studied Caribbean dance as an anthropologist and built the Dunham technique.

q: The Lindy Hop is associated with which New York venue?
fact: The Savoy Ballroom in Harlem was the home of the Lindy Hop.

q: The Charleston was a craze in which decade?
fact: The Charleston swept American dance halls in the 1920s.

q: Which company did Paul Taylor found?
fact: Paul Taylor founded his modern dance company in 1954.

q: How many counts are in a standard phrase used by most commercial choreographers?
fact: Commercial and street dance are usually counted in eights.

q: What does 'cambre' describe?
choices: A bend of the upper body
fact: Cambre means arched, a bend of the torso forward, back or to the side.

q: In a ballet class, what does 'allegro' mean?
fact: Allegro covers the quick jumping sequences; petit allegro is the small, fast ones.

q: What does 'adagio' mean in class?
fact: Adagio builds control and balance through slow, sustained movement.

q: A traditional ballet class begins with what?
fact: Class starts at the barre, then moves to center, then across the floor.

q: What is a 'penche'?
choices: A deep tilt with the leg rising behind
fact: In a penche the body tilts forward as the back leg lifts past vertical.

q: In an attitude, what is the working leg doing?
fact: The attitude position was inspired by a statue of the god Mercury.

q: What does 'echappe' mean?
fact: In an echappe the feet escape from a closed position to an open one.

q: What does 'saute' mean?
fact: Saute means jumped, as in sauté in first position.

q: What does 'glissade' mean?
fact: A glissade is a gliding traveling step, often used to launch a bigger jump.

q: What does 'changement' mean?
fact: In a changement the feet change position while the dancer is in the air.

q: What is an entrechat?
choices: A jump with the legs beating
fact: In an entrechat the legs cross and beat rapidly while the dancer is airborne.

q: The Vaganova method of ballet training comes from which country?
fact: Agrippina Vaganova codified the Russian training system in the 1930s.

q: The Cecchetti method is named after a teacher from which country?
fact: Enrico Cecchetti was an Italian dancer and teacher who trained many Ballets Russes stars.

q: Which technique is known for flat backs and lateral stretches?
fact: Lester Horton built a technique around flat backs, lateral T positions and long lines.

q: Which modern technique centers on fall and recovery?
fact: Jose Limon built on Doris Humphrey's idea of fall and recovery, using weight and momentum.

q: Jazz dance grew primarily out of which tradition?
fact: Jazz dance developed from African American social and vernacular dance.

q: Who is often called the father of theatrical jazz dance?
fact: Jack Cole's work in film and nightclubs shaped the jazz dance vocabulary Fosse built on.

q: Where did krumping originate?
fact: Krumping came out of South Central Los Angeles in the early 2000s.

q: House dance grew out of club scenes in which cities?
fact: House dance developed alongside house music in Chicago and New York clubs.

q: Whacking, with its fast arm circles, came from which scene?
fact: Whacking developed in 1970s Los Angeles disco and underground club culture.

q: What is the capital of Florida?
fact: Tallahassee has been Florida's capital since 1824.

q: Miami is the seat of which county?
fact: Miami is the county seat of Miami-Dade County.

q: Which Miami neighborhood is famous for its street art walls?
fact: The Wynwood Walls opened in 2009 and turned the district into an outdoor mural gallery.

q: The Miami Heat play in which league?
fact: The Miami Heat joined the NBA as an expansion team in 1988.

q: What is the southernmost city in the Florida Keys?
fact: Key West sits at the end of the Overseas Highway.

q: Everglades National Park is in which state?
fact: The Everglades is the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States.

q: Miami Beach is known for which architectural style?
fact: South Beach holds one of the world's largest concentrations of Art Deco buildings.

q: What is Florida's nickname?
fact: Florida adopted the Sunshine State as its official nickname in 1970.

q: Which ocean lies directly east of Miami?
fact: Miami sits on the Atlantic coast of southern Florida.

q: What is the capital of France?
fact: Paris has been France's capital since the tenth century.

q: What is the capital of Canada?
fact: Ottawa was chosen as capital by Queen Victoria in 1857.

q: What is the capital of Australia?
fact: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

q: What is the capital of Brazil?
fact: Brasilia was built inland and became the capital in 1960.

q: What is the capital of Japan?
fact: Tokyo became the capital in 1868, replacing Kyoto.

q: Which continent has the most countries?
fact: Africa has 54 sovereign countries.

q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
fact: The Pacific covers about a third of the planet's surface.

q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
fact: The Sahara spans roughly 3.6 million square miles across North Africa.

q: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies in which country?
fact: About 60 percent of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil.

q: Which is the highest mountain above sea level?
fact: Everest rises about 29,032 feet above sea level.

q: At what temperature does water freeze in Celsius?
fact: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, which is 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

q: At sea level, water boils at what Celsius temperature?
fact: Boiling point drops as altitude increases and pressure falls.

q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
fact: Babies are born with around 270 bones, and many fuse as they grow.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
fact: Skin accounts for roughly 15 percent of body weight.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
fact: Two atria on top and two ventricles below.

q: What does DNA stand for?
fact: DNA carries the genetic instructions of living organisms.

q: What gas do plants release during photosynthesis?
fact: Plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a byproduct.

q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
fact: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

q: What is the chemical formula for water?
fact: Two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
fact: Mercury orbits the Sun in about 88 Earth days.

q: Which planet is known as the red planet?
fact: Iron oxide in the soil gives Mars its rusty color.

q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
fact: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
fact: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat near 465 degrees Celsius.

q: How many natural satellites does Earth have?
fact: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
fact: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the surface on July 20, 1969.

q: Who formulated the law of universal gravitation?
fact: Newton published it in the Principia in 1687.

q: Who is credited with the equation E equals mc squared?
fact: Einstein published the mass-energy equivalence in 1905.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
fact: The exact figure is 299,792,458 meters per second.

q: What is the sound produced by lightning called?
fact: Thunder is the shock wave from air heated rapidly by the lightning channel.

q: What is a group of lions called?
fact: A pride usually contains related females, their cubs and a few males.

q: What is the fastest land animal?
fact: Cheetahs can reach around 70 miles per hour in short bursts.

q: What is the largest animal on Earth?
fact: Blue whales can reach nearly 100 feet long.

q: Dolphins belong to which class of animals?
fact: Dolphins breathe air, are warm blooded and nurse their young.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
fact: Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.

q: Why are flamingos pink?
fact: Pigments called carotenoids in algae and shrimp turn their feathers pink.

q: What word describes something that reads the same forward and backward?
fact: Level and racecar are palindromes.

q: A synonym is a word that has what?
fact: Antonyms, by contrast, mean the opposite.

q: What does 'ubiquitous' mean?
fact: It comes from the Latin ubique, meaning everywhere.

q: What does 'ephemeral' mean?
fact: Mayflies are the classic example of an ephemeral creature.

q: What does 'serendipity' mean?
fact: The word was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754.

q: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
fact: Old English once used additional letters such as thorn and eth.

q: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
fact: Shakespeare wrote the play in the mid-1590s.

q: Who wrote the Harry Potter novels?
fact: The first book was published in the UK in 1997.

q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
fact: The painting hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

q: Who painted The Starry Night?
fact: Van Gogh painted it in 1889 from his room at an asylum in Saint-Remy.

q: Which composer continued writing music after losing his hearing?
fact: Beethoven completed his Ninth Symphony while almost completely deaf.

q: How many keys does a standard full-size piano have?
fact: A standard piano has 52 white keys and 36 black keys.

q: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
fact: Bass guitars usually have four.

q: The Grammy Awards honor achievement in what field?
fact: The first Grammy Awards ceremony was held in 1959.

q: The Academy Awards are also known as what?
fact: The Tony Awards honor Broadway theater instead.

q: Who directed the 1997 film Titanic?
fact: Titanic won eleven Academy Awards.

q: The Beatles formed in which English city?
fact: The band formed in Liverpool in 1960.

q: Taylor Swift's album 1989 is named after what?
fact: Taylor Swift was born on December 13, 1989.

q: How often are the Summer Olympic Games normally held?
fact: The Tokyo 2020 Games were postponed to 2021 because of the pandemic.

q: Which city hosted the 2024 Summer Olympics?
fact: Paris previously hosted in 1900 and 1924.

q: How many players from one team are on a basketball court at a time?
fact: Basketball was invented by James Naismith in 1891.

q: How long is a marathon?
fact: The distance was fixed at 42.195 kilometers at the 1908 London Olympics.

q: In tennis, what does 'love' mean?
fact: A game score of 40-love means one player has no points.

q: How many cards are in a standard deck without jokers?
fact: Four suits of thirteen cards each.

q: How many faces does a Rubik's Cube have?
fact: Erno Rubik invented the puzzle in 1974.

q: How many days are in a leap year?
fact: The extra day is February 29, added in most years divisible by four.

q: Which country has the largest population in the world?
fact: India passed China as the most populous country in 2023.

q: What is the currency used in most of the European Union?
fact: The euro entered circulation as cash in 2002.

q: Which river is traditionally considered the longest in the world?
fact: The Nile runs roughly 4,130 miles through northeast Africa.

q: How many continents are usually taught in the English-speaking world?
fact: Some countries teach six by combining the Americas.

q: What is the main language spoken in Brazil?
fact: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world.

q: What does the Statue of Liberty hold in her raised hand?
fact: Her other arm holds a tablet inscribed with July 4, 1776.

q: Which US state is the largest by land area?
fact: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas.

q: Which sea creature is known for regrowing lost arms?
fact: Many sea stars can regenerate an arm, and some can regrow a whole body from one.

q: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?
fact: Diamond sits at 10, the top of the Mohs hardness scale.

q: Honey is produced by which insect?
fact: Sealed honey can keep for years because of its low moisture and acidity.
